To determine the supremum of \(\int_{Z(v)} dS\), we consider the properties of the function \(v\) and its gradient on the boundary \(\partial B\).

Let \(v \in C^\infty(\overline{B})\) be a real-valued harmonic function in \(B\). The vector field \(F = \nabla v = (\partial_{x_1} v, \partial_{x_2} v, \partial_{x_3} v)\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{div} F = \Delta v = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \operatorname{curl} F = 0 \quad \text{in } B,
\]
which means that \(F\) forms a generalized Cauchy–Riemann system (a Riesz system, or a monogenic function in the framework of Clifford analysis) in the unit ball \(B \subset \mathbb{R}^3\). 

By definition of the set
\[
Z(v) = \{x \in \partial B : v(x) = \partial_{x_1}v(x) = \partial_{x_2}v(x) = \partial_{x_3}v(x) = 0\},
\]
we have \(F(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in Z(v)\). 

By the boundary uniqueness theorem (the generalization of Privalov's theorem to Riesz systems / monogenic functions in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)), if a nonzero system satisfying \(\operatorname{div} F = 0\) and \(\operatorname{curl} F = 0\) extends smoothly to the boundary and vanishes on a boundary set of positive surface area measure, then \(F \equiv 0\) in \(B\). 

Since \(v\) is assumed to be nonzero and vanishes at points of \(Z(v)\), \(F = \nabla v\) cannot be identically zero (as that would imply \(v\) is constant, and hence identically zero). Consequently, the set \(Z(v)\) must have surface area measure zero with respect to \(dS\):
\[
\int_{Z(v)} dS = 0
\]
for every nonzero \(v\) satisfying the given conditions. Thus, the supremum of \(\int_{Z(v)} dS\) over all such functions is \(0\).
